catalog_quote: Several facts of Kivunjo tonology indicate the presence of accent in addition to tone. The Kivunjo accent is unlike that of more typical accentual languages in that it has no overt phonetic manifestation. Rather, it serves an organizational function, along with phonological phrasing. All p-level tone rules are directly ... Accent Rule: Assign accent to a lexical stem, choosing the penult if possible. Stem = lexical root (N, V, A) + derivational suffixes ... A lexical stem comprises a lexical root plus any derivational suffixes, but usually not including any prefixes. If a lexical stem consists of just one syllable, that syllable receives accent, even though there is no penult. This is not unusual: monosyllablic content words are ... stress, e.g., English, Latin, Indonesian, Lakhota, and Polish. With the addition of prefixes to stems, the distinction between monosyllabic and ... some stem classes are lexical exceptions to the Accent Rule, producing a third option: no accent. (22) Three accent types a. Word-penultimate accent: words with stems of two or more syllables b. Word-final accent: words with monosyllabic stems
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Vunjo (vunj1238) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title had one item, Philippson 1991 (thèse d'Etat, Paris V, 'Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale'). theses.fr marks it accessible='non', HAL and archive.org have no copy, but the author's DDL-Lyon page links the full 542-page PDF (text present), which I downloaded to and. It is directly relevant: sec. 3.12.3 (pp. 384-392) treats the Vunjo dialect, describing a fully tonal system plus a demarcative accent - stems accented on the penult (the great majority), on the final (monosyllabic and contracted stems; p. 289 'tous les thèmes monosyllabiques en chaga portent l'accent sur leur unique syllabe'), or unaccented (ethnonyms) - whose only realisation is H/super-high tone at prosodic-group end ('toute distinction accentuelle disparaît pour les mots situés en position interne de groupe', p. 387); the appendix fiche (pp. 512-513) codes Vunjo as 'langue tonale, avec accent lexical partiellement libre' with the penult's status 'accent démarcatif (culmination de longueur)'. No phonetic word stress is claimed anywhere. This confirms, in full open text, the earlier reading's classification drawn from McHugh 1990 snippets (tone language; abstract stem-penultimate accent with no overt phonetic manifestation); Philippson's data are largely McHugh's re-analysed, with his own Chaga fieldwork behind it. There being no catalog record, the item bears 'no-catalog-record'; nothing remains to acquire for this item.

All four stretches of the quote are there word for word: "Kivunjo tonology indicate the presence of accent in addi- tion to tone. The Kivunjo accent is unlike that of more typical accentual languages in that it has no overt phonetic manifestation. Rather, it serves an organizational function, along with phonological phrasing. All p - level tone rules are directly.."; "Accent Rule : Assign accent to a lexical stem, choosing the penult if possible. Stem = lexical root ( N, V, A) + derivational suffixes.."; "derivational suffixes, but usually not including any prefixes. If a lexical stem consists of just one syllable,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Vunjo is a tone language (lexical H vs L/toneless; Super-High, H and L plus contours at utterance level; rightward tone shift). McHugh posits an abstract accent on the penultimate syllable of the lexical stem (root + derivational suffixes, prefixes excluded); a monosyllabic stem is accented on its only syllable, so the accent is word-final there; some stem classes are lexically unaccented. The accent has no direct phonetic correlate (no stress); it is a diacritic that organizes phrase-level tone rules, in particular the raising of the last accented H in a phonological phrase to Super-High (Downing 2004:129; Philippson & Montlahuc 2003:480).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; no phonetic stress is claimed at all.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically unaccented stem classes ('a third option: no accent'); monosyllabic stems accented on the stem syllable, not the prefix (word-final accent).
new_statements.domain_note: Accent is assigned at stem/word level but is only detectable through phrase-level tone rules (Super-High raising of the last accent of a phonological phrase); Philippson & Montlahuc 2003 note that a toneless noun such as 'ama 'meat' gets H(F) 'and accent, in McHugh's analysis' only when final in its phonological phrase. Vunjo's four phonetic pitch levels are cited by Odden 1988 as the non-accentual tonal extreme of Bantu, opposite Swahili penultimate stress.
new_statements.identity_note: McHugh's data come from the Kirua sub-dialect of Vunjo (his 1985 UCLA MA thesis is titled 'Phrasal tone rules in Kirua (Vunjo) Chaga'); Philippson & Montlahuc 2003 label McHugh's variety 'W.' (Wunjo). Glottolog vunj1238 lists dialects Mamba (mamb1298), Marangu (mara1391), Mwika (mwik1238); Kirua is not listed separately. The other opened primary source, Nurse & Philippson 1977 'Tones in Old Moshi', describes the sister language Mochi (moch1256), not Vunjo, and is silent on stress.

new_statements.quote: Pour chaque schème tonal (BB, HB, BH, HH et aussi HBB [...]), on peut opposer thèmes accentués sur la pénultième, sur la finale, ou non-accentués. La première catégorie est de loin la plus nombreuse, la deuxième comprend essentiellement les thèmes monosyllabiques ou ceux issus d'une contraction [...] toute distinction accentuelle disparaît pour les mots situés en position interne de groupe - ce qui est logique pour un accent démarcatif ne pouvant se réaliser qu'en fin de groupe
new_statements.translation: For each tonal pattern (LL, HL, LH, HH and also HLL [...]), one can contrast stems accented on the penult, on the final, or unaccented. The first category is by far the largest; the second comprises essentially monosyllabic stems or those resulting from a contraction [...] every accentual distinction disappears for words in group-internal position - which is logical for a demarcative accent that can only be realised at the end of a group
new_statements.citation: Philippson, Gérard. 1991. Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale: étude comparative typologique et diachronique. Thèse de Doctorat d'Etat, Université Paris V. Sec. 3.12.3 'Le chaga (dialecte vunjo)', pp. 385-387 (thesis TOC: p. 378).
new_statements.locator: pp. 385-386 and 387 (PDF pages 385-387; sec. 3.12.3); confirmed by Annexe p. 512-513 (Groupe XXI, Vunjo: '3. langue tonale, avec accent lexical partiellement libre.. 10. accent démarcatif (culmination de longueur)')
new_statements.reading: Vunjo is a tone language (H/L with tone shift and super-high tones) with an abstract, lexically assigned accent that falls on the stem penult by default, on the stem's only syllable for monosyllabic stems (hence word-final), and is absent in a small class (ethnonyms). This accent has no phonetic realisation of its own word-internally or group-internally; it surfaces only at the end of a prosodic group as H/super-high tone on the accented syllable, and the appendix additionally codes the phrase penult as a demarcative accent realised by length culmination. No phonetic word stress is claimed. This is the same analysis as McHugh 1990 (Philippson re-analyses McHugh's data and adds his own Chaga knowledge) but is now available in full open text rather than Google Books snippets.

sources.note: pp. 118-119: lists 'STEM-penultimate in Chaga (McHugh 1989)' as evidence for metrical accent in Bantu: a phrase-level rule raises a stem-penultimate H; with a monosyllabic stem the stem syllable, not the prefix, undergoes it; 'only the LAST accent of a phrase will have this tone-raising effect'. On the basis of such tonal evidence, the verb phrase in (4a) would be phrased in output structure as (4b), with the direct object NP separated into a distinct MaP from the preceding indirect object. (4) a. [[ ámuénenga]V [ prayáni ]NP [ mbúru ]NP ]VP b. ( amúenénga prayání )MaP ( mburû )MaP '(S)he has given Brian a goat.'
